title: Bartter vs Gitelman Syndromes: Loop vs DCT Transporters and Urinary Calcium
subject: ss-paediatric-nephrology
module: Tubular Disorders, Cystic Diseases and Stones

steps.say: Bartter and Gitelman syndromes share hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with normal or low systemic blood pressure.
steps.tx: Recognize the unifying hemodynamic and electrolyte features of **Metabolic alkalosis and blood pressure phenotype** in inherited tubulopathies. Both Bartter and Gitelman syndromes feature hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with normal or low blood pressure despite marked hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism. Renal salt wasting stimulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, driving distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion excretion.

left.title: Shared Clinical Phenotype
points: Normal or low blood pressure (salt wasting)
High plasma renin activity and aldosterone

right.title: Distinguishing Features
points: Transporter defect: Loop of Henle vs Distal tubule

steps.say: Bartter syndrome results from mutations in transport proteins located within the thick ascending limb of Henle.
steps.tx: Map molecular genetics to the comprehensive **Bartter syndrome molecular classification (Types I-V)** across nephron segments. Bartter syndrome impairs thick ascending limb sodium chloride reabsorption: Type I results from SLC12A1 (NKCC2 cotransporter) mutations, Type II from KCNJ1 (apical ROMK potassium channel), Type III from CLCNKB (basolateral ClC-Kb chloride channel), Type IV from BSND (Barttin subunit, causing sensorineural deafness), and Type V from gain-of-function CASR mutations.

rows: Antenatal Bartter, transient hyperkalemia at birth

steps.say: Antenatal Bartter syndrome presents with maternal polyhydramnios, severe prematurity, and neonatal salt wasting.
steps.tx: Identify early perinatal manifestations characteristic of **Antenatal Bartter syndrome presentation** in neonatal care units. Antenatal Bartter (Types I and II) presents with severe maternal polyhydramnios requiring repeated amnioreductions, extreme preterm delivery, life-threatening neonatal salt wasting, profound hyposthenuria, and rapid development of medullary nephrocalcinosis within the first weeks of life.

steps.say: Gitelman syndrome stems from mutations in the thiazide-sensitive sodium chloride cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule.
steps.tx: Understand the pathophysiology of **Gitelman syndrome SLC12A3 and NCCT defect** in school-age children. Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in SLC12A3 encoding the thiazide-sensitive sodium chloride cotransporter (NCCT) in the distal convoluted tubule. This replicates the pharmacological effects of chronic thiazide diuretic use, manifesting typically in school-age children or adolescents with muscle cramps, fatigue, and salt craving.

steps.say: Urinary calcium excretion provides the decisive clinical biomarker that cleanly differentiates Bartter from Gitelman syndrome.
steps.tx: Order spot urine electrolytes to evaluate **Urinary calcium-to-creatinine differentiation** between these inherited conditions. Urinary calcium excretion cleanly differentiates the two disorders: Bartter syndrome causes hypercalciuria (urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio > 0.2 mg/mg) due to loss of the lumen-positive transepithelial potential in the thick ascending limb, whereas Gitelman syndrome causes marked hypocalciuria (urine Ca/Cr ratio < 0.1 mg/mg).

steps.say: Severe persistent hypomagnesemia caused by TRPM6 channel down-regulation represents the hallmark of Gitelman syndrome.
steps.tx: Recognize the metabolic consequences of **Hypomagnesemia in Gitelman syndrome** in symptomatic adolescents. Severe persistent hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium < 1.7 mg/dL) due to down-regulation of TRPM6 epithelial magnesium channels in the atrophied distal convoluted tubule is a classic hallmark of Gitelman syndrome. Clinical manifestations include recurrent carpopedal spasms, muscle tetany, chondrocalcinosis, and cardiac arrhythmias.

steps.say: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents block renal prostaglandin synthesis to attenuate excessive polyuria and salt wasting.
steps.tx: Prescribe cyclooxygenase inhibitors as **Indomethacin therapy in Bartter syndrome** to stabilize electrolyte losses. Excessive renal prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) production drives hyperreninemia and profound polyuria in Bartter syndrome. Cyclooxygenase inhibitors (indomethacin at 1.5-3.0 mg/kg/day or celecoxib) close this feedback loop, markedly reducing polyuria, improving glomerular filtration rate, and stabilizing serum potassium and chloride levels.

nodes.label: Reduces Polyuria, GFR Normalization & Electrolyte Retention

steps.say: Potassium-sparing diuretics supplement potassium chloride repletion to counteract secondary hyperaldosteronism.
steps.tx: Administer combination electrolyte management through **Potassium-sparing diuretics add-on** in severe hypokalemic states. High-dose oral potassium chloride repletion is supplemented with potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone at 2-4 mg/kg/day, amiloride, or eplerenone) to counteract secondary hyperaldosteronism. This approach diminishes kaliuresis and stabilizes systemic potassium concentrations while monitoring for signs of dehydration.
